context: The prompt requests changing the git commit timing during the archiving workflow. Currently, the commit happens after creating the zip archive but before deleting the workdir contents. The prompt states the commit should be after both zip creation and workdir deletion. This questionnaire clarifies the exact timing and safety considerations for this change.

questions.question-text: At which exact point in the cleanup workflow should the git commit occur?

options.label: After workdir is renamed to .deleting but before it is actually deleted
options.pros: Provides a safety checkpoint where the commit is made but rollback is still possible if deletion fails; the rename operation is atomic and reversible
options.cons: The workdir still exists on disk (though renamed) when the commit is made; if someone checks out the commit immediately, they won't see a clean empty workdir

options.label: After workdir.deleting is fully deleted but before the new empty workdir is created
options.pros: Ensures the old workdir is completely gone before committing; commit represents a clean state transition; no confusion about workdir state
options.cons: If commit fails, we're in a state with no workdir at all; requires careful error handling to recreate workdir on commit failure

options.label: After the new empty workdir is created (the very last step)
options.pros: Safest option - workdir is always in a valid state even if commit fails; commit represents the complete final state including the fresh empty workdir; easiest error recovery
options.cons: The new empty workdir folder itself becomes part of the commit, though this is the desired final state

options.label: After final verification that the new workdir is empty
options.pros: Combines safety of having a fresh workdir with verification that cleanup succeeded; commit only happens after all operations are validated; provides the most confidence in the final state
options.cons: Slightly more complex workflow; if verification fails but workdir is created, we're in an inconsistent state (though this is already caught by current error handling)

questions.recommendation-rationale: Option C provides the best balance of safety and correctness. The commit happens after the complete cleanup workflow succeeds, including creation of the fresh empty workdir. This ensures that if the commit fails, the system is still in a valid state with an empty workdir ready for new work. The fresh empty workdir being part of the commit is actually the desired final state, matching the requirements that workdir should be cleared after archiving.

questions.question-text: How should the script handle git commit failures in the new position?

options.label: Fail the entire operation and leave the fresh workdir in place but print an error
options.pros: Simple implementation; preserves the fresh workdir; user can manually commit later; no complex rollback logic needed
options.cons: The archive operation appears to have failed even though the archiving and cleanup succeeded; inconsistent state between filesystem and git

options.label: Treat git commit as optional and only log a warning if it fails
options.pros: Archive operation always succeeds regardless of git state; resilient to git configuration issues; user can manually commit later if desired
options.cons: Violates the principle that git-enabled=true means git operations should be enforced; may lead to forgotten commits; inconsistent with current behavior

options.label: Keep the current behavior: fail the entire operation if git-enabled is true and commit fails
options.pros: Maintains consistency with existing behavior; enforces git-enabled contract; ensures user is aware of commit failures immediately
options.cons: More user intervention required on git failures; successful archive and cleanup work is visible but operation is marked as failed

questions.recommendation-rationale: Option C maintains consistency with the existing behavior and requirements. The current code treats git commit failures as errors when git-enabled=true, and this behavior should be preserved. Moving the commit to a later position shouldn't change the error handling semantics. Users who enable git integration expect commits to be enforced, and failures should be visible.
